concepts.title: Collecting and Storing Data
concepts.explanation:
Before you can manage data, you have to collect it. And before you collect it, you have to plan. Good data managers never just grab numbers randomly; they think carefully about what they want to find out and how they will find it out. This careful, planned way of collecting data is called a statistical investigation.

What is a statistical investigation?

A statistical investigation is when we collect data to answer a question. The data we collect is called statistics. For example, an ice-cream shop owner might ask, 'Which flavour of ice cream is the most popular?' To find out, she counts how many scoops of each flavour she sells, and then she analyses that data. To analyse data means to look closely at it, find patterns in it, and think carefully about what it means. This is useful, because once she knows the most popular flavour she can buy more of it and never run out.
concepts.example: In our scenario, Leila is doing a statistical investigation. Her question is, 'What is the favourite fruit of the learners in my class?' She will collect data from her classmates, store it neatly, and then analyse it to find the answer.

concepts.title: Data and information are not the same
concepts.explanation:
Here is an idea that many people get muddled, so read it slowly. Data is meaningless facts or figures on their own, like the number 7 or the word green. By itself, green does not tell you anything useful. Information is data that has been given meaning. When we say 'green is the most popular colour in the class', that is information, because now the fact means something. Managing data well is really the art of turning plain data into useful information.

Here is the key difference to remember. Discrete data is counted and is always a whole value — you cannot have half a pet or three-and-a-bit customers. Continuous data is measured and can be any value at all, like a temperature of 24.5 degrees or a height of 1.42 metres. In Leila's fruit investigation, the type of fruit ('mango', 'banana') is categorical, and the number of learners who chose each fruit is discrete. In Zane's temperature investigation, each reading is continuous.

Before you collect a single number, ask yourself four planning questions. Answering them first saves you a lot of trouble later.

What data do I want to collect? For example, 'the favourite fruit of each learner in my class'.

How will I collect the data? With a form, a data logger, a survey, or a spreadsheet.

How will I organise the data? Usually by putting it into a spreadsheet in a sensible order.
concepts.example: How will I use the data to get information? Perhaps by counting, calculating, and drawing a chart to make the pattern clear.

concepts.title: The tools we use to collect and store data
concepts.explanation:
Humans are not very good at collecting and organising lots of data by hand — we forget things, make mistakes, and it takes ages. Computers are far better: they do not forget, and they measure and calculate very quickly. Here are the most useful computing tools for a statistical investigation.

Data loggers — a data logger is a device that reads and records data from the world automatically (by itself, with no human help) and continuously (carrying on until you tell it to stop). It uses sensors. For example, a data logger could record the temperature of a fish tank every five minutes, all day and night. Data loggers are excellent for collecting continuous data like temperature, light level or a person's pulse.

Spreadsheets — such as LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet stores data in a neat grid of cells, and it can add up columns, do other calculations, and draw charts in an instant. It is designed to make working with numbers easy.

Databases — a database stores related data of many types (not just numbers) in an organised way. It can be paper-based, like a diary or calendar, or digital. Databases make it easy to find, sort and analyse data, and they can hold enormous amounts — far more than a spreadsheet.

Forms — a form is a list of questions with spaces for people to mark or write their answers. A good form makes people enter their data in the same way, so it is easy to organise. Forms can be on paper or on a screen.

Document production tools — word processors and presentation programs let you put text and pictures together to make a report or a presentation, which is a good way to share the results of your investigation.

A data logger works day and night without ever getting tired or bored.

Scientists put data loggers in places no human could stay, like the top of a mountain or the bottom of the sea, and leave them for months to record the temperature or the weather all by themselves.

Some hotels use data loggers in a control system: when the temperature reaches 23 degrees a cooling system switches on by itself, and if it falls to 18 degrees the heating turns on.

Let us help Leila. Her question is, 'What is the favourite fruit in my class?' She designs a simple form with one clear question — 'What is your favourite fruit?' — and a list of choices to tick: Mango, Banana, Orange, Watermelon, Dates, and a space for 'other'. Giving people a list of choices is clever, because it stops one person writing 'mango', another writing 'Mangoes' and another writing 'MANGO' — which would be three different answers to the computer, even though they mean the same fruit.

After every classmate has filled in the form, Leila counts up the answers and stores them in a LibreOffice Calc spreadsheet. She organises the data in two columns — the fruit, and the number of learners who chose it — and sorts it from most popular to least popular:
concepts.example: Now the data has become information. Leila can see straight away that mango is the favourite fruit in her class, chosen by 9 learners, and that dates were chosen by the fewest. The type of fruit is categorical data, and the number of learners who chose each fruit is discrete data. If Leila adds up the numbers 9 + 6 + 4 + 4 + 2, she finds that 25 learners answered her form altogether.

concepts.title: A free, open
concepts.explanation:
Some online form tools need an account and are not free or open-source. You do not need them! You can build a tidy digital data-entry form right inside LibreOffice Calc, using its validation rules. A validation rule is like a helpful gatekeeper: it only lets good data in. Here is how Leila makes the fruit column accept only the fruits on her list:

Type the heading Fruit in cell A1.

Select the cells where people will enter data, for example A2:A26.

On the Criteria tab, set Allow to List.

In the Entries box, type the choices, one per line: Mango, Banana, Orange, Watermelon, Dates.

Click OK. Now every one of those cells shows a little drop-down arrow, and nobody can type a fruit that is not on the list or misspell one by accident.
concepts.example: This is exactly how the online form's drop-down list works, but it is free and open-source and needs no account at all.

concepts.title: Restricting cells
concepts.explanation:
It is very easy to enter data incorrectly. If Zara typed a birthday as 3112 instead of 31/12, she would never find that birthday again when she searched. If Karim typed ouzzle instead of puzzle, the spreadsheet would treat it as a different word. Validation rules limit the kind of data a cell will accept, and this stops many of these mistakes before they happen. In LibreOffice Calc you set them with Data > Validity. A cell can be made to accept:

only decimal numbers, for example a temperature;

only text from a list you provide, like a drop-down of Yes and No;

only numbers between two limits, for example a score from 1 to 5 (so the cell would refuse a 6).

Imagine Zane is scoring the school lunch out of 5. He selects the score column, opens Data > Validity, sets Allow to Whole Numbers, the condition to between, Minimum 1 and Maximum 5. On the Error Alert tab he chooses the Stop action. Now the cell politely refuses any score below 1 or above 5, and even refuses a word — so his data stays clean and correct.

concepts.title: Representing Data
concepts.explanation:
Once you have collected some data, you can represent it — that is, show it — in different ways. A good representation makes the meaning of the data leap out at you. In this subunit you will learn to represent data in tables, bar charts and line graphs, and you will learn to calculate with formulas and functions in LibreOffice Calc.

The simplest way to represent data is in a table of rows and columns, exactly like a spreadsheet. A table makes it easy to see which pieces of data go together. Here is a table Leila made about how the 24 learners in her class travel to school:

By reading the table we get information: most learners walk to school, and very few come by car. If we add up the numbers 12 + 9 + 3 we get 24, the whole class. Because 12 is half of 24, we can even say that half the class walks to school. A table like this is much easier to read than the same facts written out in a long sentence.

But a table is not always enough. Imagine a table showing the eye colour of everyone in a big city, with numbers like 252780, 344700 and 574500. Those numbers are so big that it is hard to get a clear picture of which is largest. This is exactly when a chart becomes useful.
concepts.example: A chart (or graph) is like a picture of your data. Charts make it much quicker and easier to see patterns and to summarise information. There are several kinds, and a good data manager chooses the kind that best suits the data. The two you will use most are the bar chart and the line graph.

concepts.title: Bar charts
concepts.explanation:
A bar chart has a separate coloured bar for each category. The longer the bar, the greater the value. Because bar charts work by counting how many times each option is chosen, they are perfect for categorical data (like favourite fruit) and discrete data (like a number of votes). Here is Leila's fruit data again, ready to become a bar chart:

On the bar chart, mango would have the tallest bar and dates the shortest. You can see the winner in a single glance, without reading any numbers at all. To make this chart in LibreOffice Calc, Leila follows these steps:

Select the data, including the headings: click and drag across the Fruit column and the Number column together.

Open the menu Insert > Chart. The Chart Wizard appears.

In Step 1 — Choose a Chart Type, pick Column for bars that stand up tall (or Bar for bars that lie sideways). Click Next.

In Steps 2 and 3, make sure 'First row as label' and 'First column as label' are ticked, then click Next.

In Step 4 — Chart Elements, type a clear Title such as 'Favourite fruit in our class', label the axes, and tick Display legend. Click Finish.

Click anywhere outside the chart to leave edit mode. Your bar chart is done!

More than half of all the people in the world have brown eyes — that is around 4 billion people!
concepts.example: Different countries have very different eye-colour patterns, so a chart of eye colour in one country can look quite different from a chart in another.

concepts.title: The parts of a chart
concepts.explanation:
Bar charts and line graphs have two lines called axes. The y axis goes up and down (it is vertical) and usually shows the scale, like the number of learners. The x axis goes from side to side (it is horizontal) and usually shows the categories or the time. The title you put on each axis is called a label, and labels explain what each axis measures. The little key that tells you what each colour means is called the legend. A chart without labels is like a letter with no address — nobody can be sure what it means.

Bar charts can be drawn two ways. A column chart has vertical bars going up; a bar chart in LibreOffice has horizontal bars going across. Both show the same information — you simply choose whichever is easier to read.

Line graphs: for continuous data

A line graph is best for continuous data that changes over time, because the sloping lines show you how the data rises and falls between the points. Let us help Zane. He set up a data logger to record the temperature in his Mogadishu classroom every hour. This is his data:

To draw this by hand, you would mark a dot for each temperature at the right height above its time, then join the dots with straight lines. LibreOffice Calc does it for you: select the data, choose Insert > Chart, and pick the Line chart type in the wizard. The finished line climbs from the cool early morning up to a peak at 32 degrees at 1 o'clock, then slopes back down as the afternoon cools. The shape of the line tells the story instantly, which is why Zane chooses the club's outdoor games for the cooler early morning. This temperature data is a perfect example of continuous data.

Why not use a bar chart for this? Because temperature flows smoothly from one reading to the next, and the lines show that flow. And why not use a line graph for favourite fruit? Because the fruits are separate categories, not a smooth change over time — joining 'mango' to 'banana' with a line would make no sense at all. Choosing the right chart is a real skill.

Sometimes you make a chart and then realise a different kind would be clearer. Happily, this is easy to change in LibreOffice Calc: double-click the chart to enter edit mode, then right-click it and choose Chart Type, pick Line (or Column), and click OK. Click outside to finish. You can also change the style and labels to suit who will read the chart. Good choices matter:

For a reader who is colour-blind and cannot tell red from green, choose different colours (like blue and orange) or add clear labels to each line, so the colours are not the only clue.

For a chart shown on a small screen, keep it simple: a summary with big, clear text.

For a chart shown on a big screen to a whole room, you can show lots of detail and many data points.

You can change the title, the axis labels, the gridlines, the colours and the size of the text to make any chart clearer.

A spreadsheet is also a brilliant calculator. In maths you already use operators — the symbols for calculations. In a spreadsheet, some of the symbols are different, so learn these four carefully:

The two to watch are multiply and divide. On paper you write 6 x 4, but in a spreadsheet you type an asterisk: =6*4, which returns 24. On paper you write a division sign, but in a spreadsheet you type a forward slash: =20/4, which returns 5.
concepts.example: A formula is an instruction to do a calculation, and in a spreadsheet a formula must always begin with an equals sign =. The = tells LibreOffice Calc, 'Do not treat this as ordinary text — work it out for me.' The real magic is that instead of typing a number in a formula, you usually type a cell reference — the address of the cell where that number lives, like A1 or B3. Look at this tiny example:

concepts.title: A formula that uses cell references
concepts.explanation:
The formula =A1+A2 means 'the value in cell A1 plus the value in cell A2'. It shows 9. Here is the clever part: if you later change A1 from 3 to 5, the result in A3 updates all by itself to 11. You never have to work it out again. Because of this, always put a formula in a cell of its own, not in one of the cells you are calculating with.

Sometimes a formula would be very long. Imagine adding up twenty test scores with + signs — it would take ages and be easy to get wrong. That is why spreadsheets have functions: ready-made calculations built into the software. To use one, type =, then the function name, then the cell range in brackets. A range is all the cells between and including two cells, written with a colon : that means 'to'. So B2:B6 means every cell from B2 to B6. The two functions you will use most are:

The two functions you will use most

=SUM(B2:B6) adds up every value from B2 to B6

=AVERAGE(B2:B6) finds the average (mean) of every value from B2 to B6
concepts.example: The SUM function adds up all the values in the range. The AVERAGE function finds the average: it adds up the values and then divides by how many there are. For example, for the four values 3, 7, 4, 6, the average is 3 + 7 + 4 + 6 = 20, then 20 / 4 = 5. So the average is 5.

concepts.title: Worked example: Ehel Academy test scores
concepts.explanation:
The class has done three maths tests this term, each marked out of 10. Their teacher types the marks into LibreOffice Calc and wants to work out each learner's total and percentage, and the total and average for each test. Here is the data:

First, the total for each learner. In cell E2 you type =B2+C2+D2 and press Enter; it shows 24, because 8 + 7 + 9 = 24. You can copy this formula down to E6 (select E2 and press Ctrl+D, or drag the little handle at the corner of the cell). LibreOffice cleverly changes the row numbers for you, so E3 becomes =B3+C3+D3. Here are all the totals:

Column E: each learner's total out of 30

Next, the percentage. Each learner could score 30 in total (10 on each of the three tests), so the percentage is the total divided by 30. In cell F2 you type =E2/30. This shows 0.8 at first, because 24 divided by 30 is 0.8. To make it look like a percentage, keep F2 selected and click the percentage button (marked %) on the Formatting toolbar. Now it shows 80.00%. Leila scored 80%. Nora scored 28/30, which is 0.9333..., or 93.33% — and that is why some percentages have decimal places, because 28 does not divide evenly by 30.
concepts.example: Now the teacher wants the total and the average for each test, using functions. She puts the totals in row 7 and the averages in row 8:

concepts.title: Average of Test 1
concepts.explanation:
Average of Test 2: in C8 type =AVERAGE(C2:C6) -> 8

Average of Test 3: in D8 type =AVERAGE(D2:D6) -> 8.2

Let us check by hand so you can see the software is right. Test 1 scores are 8, 6, 9, 7 and 10, which add up to 40; divide by the 5 learners and the average is 8. Test 3 scores are 9, 7, 8, 8 and 9, which add up to 41; divide by 5 and the average is 8.2. The .2 is a decimal because 41 does not divide evenly by 5 — this is completely normal for an average. Everything the spreadsheet worked out matches our pencil-and-paper check.

A single LibreOffice Calc spreadsheet has 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns.

That is more than 17 billion cells in one sheet — far more than anyone could ever fill by hand.

Calc also has more than 500 ready-made functions waiting for you, though SUM and AVERAGE are the two you will use most this year.

concepts.title: Using Data
concepts.explanation:
You can now collect data, store it, represent it and calculate with it. In this last subunit you will learn two more powerful skills: what happens when you change data in a spreadsheet, and how to find exactly the data you need in a big spreadsheet in seconds. Then you will put everything together in a real investigation.

What happens when we change data?
concepts.example: Sometimes we need to change the data in a spreadsheet — maybe we spot a mistake, or we get new information, or a price changes. Spreadsheets are very clever about this. When you change a piece of data, every formula and every chart that uses that data updates instantly, all by itself. You never have to redo your calculations or redraw your charts by hand.

concepts.title: Worked example: Aunt Nora's juice shop in Hargeisa
concepts.explanation:
Aunt Nora recorded, for one week, how many customers came into her juice shop each day and how much money she took, all in Somali shillings. She uses a formula to work out the average spend per customer each day: the takings divided by the number of customers. Here is her spreadsheet:

Column D divides the takings by the customers to find the average spend. For example, D4 is =C4/B4, which is 150000 / 25 = 6000 shillings per customer on Monday. Nora can also find her weekly totals with SUM: =SUM(B2:B8) gives 255 customers for the week, and =SUM(C2:C8) gives 1480000 shillings taken for the week.
concepts.example: Now watch what happens when data changes. Nora realises she forgot to count 5 customers who came in on Monday while she stepped out — there were really 30, not 25. She clicks cell B4, types 30, and presses Enter. Instantly, two things update by themselves:

concepts.title: Changing one cell updates every formula that uses it
concepts.explanation:
Before: B4 = 25 -> D4 =C4/B4 = 150000 / 25 = 6000

After: B4 = 30 -> D4 =C4/B4 = 150000 / 30 = 5000

The weekly total customers =SUM(B2:B8) changes from 255 to 260.

The average spend for Monday drops from 6000 to 5000 shillings, and the weekly customer total rises from 255 to 260. But notice that the takings in cell C4 stayed exactly the same at 150000. Why? Because C4 holds a number that Nora typed in herself, not a formula — so nothing told it to change. Only cells with a formula recalculate. This is an important idea: typed values stay put, but formulas react to change.

The very same thing happens to charts. If Nora had made a bar chart of her daily customers, the Monday bar would have grown taller by itself the moment she changed 25 to 30. She never has to touch the chart. This is why spreadsheets are so powerful for a shop owner: she can try out a change and see the effect on all her totals and charts in a single second.

Spreadsheets often hold a great deal of data, and it is slow to find one thing by reading every row. Instead we use search criteria — the words or conditions we search for to find data that matches. You already use search criteria every time you type words into a search engine on the internet. Shops do this too: a supermarket can search its records for every customer who often buys dates, and then send just those customers a special offer on dates.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 2: Data and information are not the same
workedExamples.prompt: A statistical investigation is: (a) A type of chart (b) Collecting data to answer a question (c) A spreadsheet formula (d) A kind of cell
workedExamples.solution:
Here is an idea that many people get muddled, so read it slowly. Data is meaningless facts or figures on their own, like the number 7 or the word green. By itself, green does not tell you anything useful. Information is data that has been given meaning. When we say 'green is the most popular colour in the class', that is information, because now the fact means something. Managing data well is really the art of turning plain data into useful information.

Here is the key difference to remember. Discrete data is counted and is always a whole value — you cannot have half a pet or three-and-a-bit customers. Continuous data is measured and can be any value at all, like a temperature of 24.5 degrees or a height of 1.42 metres. In Leila's fruit investigation, the type of fruit ('mango', 'banana') is categorical, and the number of learners who chose each fruit is discrete. In Zane's temperature investigation, each reading is continuous.

Before you collect a single number, ask yourself four planning questions. Answering them first saves you a lot of trouble later.

What data do I want to collect? For example, 'the favourite fruit of each learner in my class'.

How will I collect the data? With a form, a data logger, a survey, or a spreadsheet.

How will I organise the data? Usually by putting it into a spreadsheet in a sensible order.

For example: How will I use the data to get information? Perhaps by counting, calculating, and drawing a chart to make the pattern clear.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 3: The tools we use to collect and store data
workedExamples.prompt: Which is an example of information, not just data? (a) The number 7 (b) The word 'green' (c) 'Green is the most popular colour' (d) The letter B
workedExamples.solution:
Humans are not very good at collecting and organising lots of data by hand — we forget things, make mistakes, and it takes ages. Computers are far better: they do not forget, and they measure and calculate very quickly. Here are the most useful computing tools for a statistical investigation.

Data loggers — a data logger is a device that reads and records data from the world automatically (by itself, with no human help) and continuously (carrying on until you tell it to stop). It uses sensors. For example, a data logger could record the temperature of a fish tank every five minutes, all day and night. Data loggers are excellent for collecting continuous data like temperature, light level or a person's pulse.

Spreadsheets — such as LibreOffice Calc. A spreadsheet stores data in a neat grid of cells, and it can add up columns, do other calculations, and draw charts in an instant. It is designed to make working with numbers easy.

Databases — a database stores related data of many types (not just numbers) in an organised way. It can be paper-based, like a diary or calendar, or digital. Databases make it easy to find, sort and analyse data, and they can hold enormous amounts — far more than a spreadsheet.

Forms — a form is a list of questions with spaces for people to mark or write their answers. A good form makes people enter their data in the same way, so it is easy to organise. Forms can be on paper or on a screen.

Document production tools — word processors and presentation programs let you put text and pictures together to make a report or a presentation, which is a good way to share the results of your investigation.

A data logger works day and night without ever getting tired or bored.

Scientists put data loggers in places no human could stay, like the top of a mountain or the bottom of the sea, and leave them for months to record the temperature or the weather all by themselves.

Some hotels use data loggers in a control system: when the temperature reaches 23 degrees a cooling system switches on by itself, and if it falls to 18 degrees the heating turns on.

Let us help Leila. Her question is, 'What is the favourite fruit in my class?' She designs a simple form with one clear question — 'What is your favourite fruit?' — and a list of choices to tick: Mango, Banana, Orange, Watermelon, Dates, and a space for 'other'. Giving people a list of choices is clever, because it stops one person writing 'mango', another writing 'Mangoes' and another writing 'MANGO' — which would be three different answers to the computer, even though they mean the same fruit.

After every classmate has filled in the form, Leila counts up the answers and stores them in a LibreOffice Calc spreadsheet. She organises the data in two columns — the fruit, and the number of learners who chose it — and sorts it from most popular to least popular:

For example: Now the data has become information. Leila can see straight away that mango is the favourite fruit in her class, chosen by 9 learners, and that dates were chosen by the fewest. The type of fruit is categorical data, and the number of learners who chose each fruit is discrete data. If Leila adds up the numbers 9 + 6 + 4 + 4 + 2, she finds that 25 learners answered her form altogether.

workedExamples.prompt: Every spreadsheet formula must begin with: (a) A colon (b) An equals sign (c) A bracket (d) A letter

It is very easy to enter data incorrectly. If Zara typed a birthday as 3112 instead of 31/12, she would never find that birthday again when she searched. If Karim typed ouzzle instead of puzzle, the spreadsheet would treat it as a different word. Validation rules limit the kind of data a cell will accept, and this stops many of these mistakes before they happen. In LibreOffice Calc you set them with Data > Validity. A cell can be made to accept:

only decimal numbers, for example a temperature;

only text from a list you provide, like a drop-down of Yes and No;

only numbers between two limits, for example a score from 1 to 5 (so the cell would refuse a 6).

Imagine Zane is scoring the school lunch out of 5. He selects the score column, opens Data > Validity, sets Allow to Whole Numbers, the condition to between, Minimum 1 and Maximum 5. On the Error Alert tab he chooses the Stop action. Now the cell politely refuses any score below 1 or above 5, and even refuses a word — so his data stays clean and correct.

Once you have collected some data, you can represent it — that is, show it — in different ways. A good representation makes the meaning of the data leap out at you. In this subunit you will learn to represent data in tables, bar charts and line graphs, and you will learn to calculate with formulas and functions in LibreOffice Calc.

The simplest way to represent data is in a table of rows and columns, exactly like a spreadsheet. A table makes it easy to see which pieces of data go together. Here is a table Leila made about how the 24 learners in her class travel to school:

By reading the table we get information: most learners walk to school, and very few come by car. If we add up the numbers 12 + 9 + 3 we get 24, the whole class. Because 12 is half of 24, we can even say that half the class walks to school. A table like this is much easier to read than the same facts written out in a long sentence.

But a table is not always enough. Imagine a table showing the eye colour of everyone in a big city, with numbers like 252780, 344700 and 574500. Those numbers are so big that it is hard to get a clear picture of which is largest. This is exactly when a chart becomes useful.

For example: A chart (or graph) is like a picture of your data. Charts make it much quicker and easier to see patterns and to summarise information. There are several kinds, and a good data manager chooses the kind that best suits the data. The two you will use most are the bar chart and the line graph.

rules.text: Data is meaningless facts on their own; information is data with meaning. Categorical = groups; discrete = whole numbers you count; continuous = any value you measure. A data logger records continuous data automatically and continuously.
Every formula starts with an equals sign: =SUM(B2:B8). In a spreadsheet, * means multiply and / means divide. The colon : means 'to', so B2:B8 means every cell from B2 to B8.

SUM adds up the values in a range. AVERAGE finds the mean of the values in a range. Only use AVERAGE on numbers, never on words like 'mango'. Put your formula in an empty cell, not in a cell you are calculating with.

Use a bar chart for categories; use a line graph for change over time. Always give a chart a clear title and label both axes. Change one number, and every formula and chart that uses it updates by itself.

Data is meaningless facts or figures on their own, like '7' or 'green'. Information is data with meaning, like 'green is the most popular colour in the class'. The whole point of managing data is to turn data into useful information. The three types of data Not all data is the same. Knowing which type you are collecting helps you choose the right tool to collect it and the right chart to show it. There are three types you need to know for this unit. Type of data

Validation rules are a helpful gatekeeper: they let good data in and keep bad data out. Data > Validity in LibreOffice Calc can force a cell to accept only whole numbers, only decimals, only dates, only times, or only items from a list. The Stop action refuses a wrong entry completely; a Warning action lets it in but warns the user first.

Every formula must start with an equals sign. No equals sign, no calculation! In a spreadsheet, * means multiply and / means divide. Use a cell reference (like B3) in a formula, and the answer updates by itself when that cell changes. Calculations using functions: SUM and AVERAGE Sometimes a formula would be very long. Imagine adding up twenty test scores with + signs — it would take ages and be easy to get wrong. That is why spreadsheets have functions: ready-made calculations built into the software. To use one, type =, then the function name, then the cell range in brackets. A range is all the cells between and including two cells, written with a colon : that means 'to'. So B2:B6 means every cell from B2 to B6. The two functions you will use most are: The two functions you will use most

Change one cell, and every formula and chart that uses it updates by itself, instantly. A cell with a formula recalculates; a cell with a typed-in value does not change on its own. This is why we use cell references in formulas instead of typing the numbers straight in. Finding specific data with search criteria Spreadsheets often hold a great deal of data, and it is slow to find one thing by reading every row. Instead we use search criteria — the words or conditions we search for to find data that matches. You already use search criteria every time you type words into a search engine on the internet. Shops do this too: a supermarket can search its records for every customer who often buys dates, and then send just those customers a special offer on dates.
